newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to act against Belgian TV ad monopoly.
newsitem.headline: EU to act against Belgian TV ad monopoly.

text.p: The European Commission, in a display of strength over fair competition in the television sector, will tell Belgium on Thursday it must scrap the advertising monopoly granted to Flemish TV channel VTM or face legal action.

It was significant that the Commission acted so quickly after EU leaders agreed at their summit in Amsterdam last week to protect public broadcasters from EU competitioon rules, a decision taken at the instigation of Belgium.

In 1989 VTM was given an 18-year advertising monopoly for Dutch-speaking Flanders, in northern Belgium, which has been attacked by rival channel VT4 owned by TV group Scandinavian Broadcasting System.
"The Commission will take an article 90 decision on Thursday against VTM," a Commission official.

Under Article 90 of the Treaty of Rome, the European Union's founding text, the Commission can force governments and companies to respect competition rules without needing to seek the advice of EU ministers.
VT4 has been forced to set up headquarters in London to circumvent VTM's monopoly and to be able to broadcast to Flanders.
The channel started operations in February 1995 despite the opposition of the Flemish regional government and took the issue to the Commission the same year.
EU governments agreed last week in Amsterdam that EU treaty provisions on fair competition should not prevent the funding of public service broadcasting.

The EU leaders were reacting to increasing complaints from private channels about subsidies paid to public broadcasters, either directly or through a TV fee, despite the fact that they also often compete for advertising revenue.

The protocol on public broadcasters was heralded by the state-controlled sector as a victory. But Commission sources and commercial TV channels said it did not mean that national governments now had a free rein on subsidies to the sector.

"The text says that the funding granted to the public service must be provided in a way which does not affect competition...it does not exclude public broadcasting from competition rules," Daniel Zimmermann, director-general of the Association of Commercial Television (ACT) in Europe, said.
Zimmermann said ACT was still assessing the legal implications of the protocol, but he thought on-going actions brought before the Commission were still valid.

French TV channel TF1, which is owned by Bouygues, has complained about France 2 and France 3. Similar actions have been filed by private Italian and Spanish channels against their public competitors.
